title: A compass bearing you can name
allegory: A feature is a compass bearing on the model's map of activations: each activation is a spot on the map, how much of the feature it holds is how far it lies along that bearing, and the bearings rarely follow the map's printed grid lines, which are the neurons.
map: an activation vector, e.g. the residual stream at one token
a compass bearing someone can name
a feature: a direction that corresponds to a human-nameable property
how far the spot lies along that bearing
the feature's activation: the dot product of the activation with the direction
the neuron basis, which features need not align with
more bearings than the map has dimensions, so some overlap
superposition: more features than dimensions, paid for with interference

chapters.name: The confusing neuron
chapters.note: why does this one neuron fire on everything?

cap.1: You open up a model and watch one neuron. It fires on several things that have nothing to do with each other. So what is the model actually tracking?
cap.2: Single neurons are often polysemantic: one unit responds to several unrelated concepts. That makes neurons a poor unit of analysis and pushes us to look for directions instead.
cap.3: Polysemanticity is an observation. The unit of analysis that survives it is a direction in activation space, not a coordinate: a basis with no privileged axes gives features no reason to align with neurons.

cap.1: Think of the model's activations as spots on a map. A feature is a compass bearing you can name, like 'towards French text'. It needn't follow the printed grid.
cap.2: A feature is a direction in activation space that corresponds to something a human can name. Neurons are just the axes the numbers happen to be written in; features can point anywhere.
cap.3: Features are directions, not basis elements. In a non-privileged space the neuron axes mean nothing special; an elementwise nonlinearity makes the basis privileged, and only then can features align with neurons.

cap.1: To ask how much of a feature a spot holds, measure how far it lies along the bearing. Far along: strongly present. At right angles: absent.
cap.2: A feature's activation is the dot product of the activation vector with the feature's unit direction. That is roughly what a linear probe or an SAE latent reads out.
cap.3: Projection onto d reads the feature: ⟨a, d⟩. Adding α·d writes it, which is what steering does. Reading and writing along the same direction is why the linear picture is so useful.

cap.1: A two-direction map can hold five bearings if they're rarely used together. They can't all be at right angles, so reading one picks up a bit of the others.
cap.2: Superposition: with sparse data a model can store more features than it has dimensions, as overlapping directions. Anthropic's toy model squeezes five features into two, and they form a pentagon.
cap.3: Elhage et al. (2022): with sparse inputs, five features in a 2D hidden space arrange as a pentagon, tolerating interference because co-occurrence is rare. Dense inputs give PCA-like behaviour instead.

chapters.name: Is it really straight?

left.title: Working assumption
lines: write them by adding a vector

right.title: Still being tested
lines: a two-meaning neuron may be one mislabelled feature
or not a feature at all

chapters.verdict: Treat features as directions, then test each one by intervening.

cap.1: Is every idea in a model a straight bearing? That's a hypothesis, not a law. What you need: treat features as directions and test each one by pushing along it.
cap.2: Current method: assume the linear representation hypothesis and hunt for directions. Open question: how far it holds. What you need: confirm a named feature by intervening along it, not only by reading examples.
cap.3: Features-as-directions is the linear representation hypothesis. A polysemantic neuron may reflect superposition, one mislabelled feature, or a mid-computation activation that is no feature at all. Test causally.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: SAEs hunt for all of them at once

cap.1: Most of interpretability is finding these bearings, reading them and pushing along them. That is how you start to understand and steer a model.
cap.2: Linear probes, sparse autoencoders and steering vectors all assume features are directions. Get this picture right and those tools become one idea used three ways.
cap.3: Superposition is why SAEs exist: to recover an overcomplete set of feature directions from a crowded residual stream, so you can read and steer the model one named direction at a time.

coda.title: Five feature bearings share two dimensions: point the activation and read each one

caption.1: The activation points along feature 1, yet features 2 and 5 light up a little: that's interference. Raise the threshold until only the true feature is left.
caption.2: Five directions share two dimensions, so they can't be perpendicular: reading one picks up about 0.31 of each neighbour. Ignoring small readings works while one feature fires at a time, which is why sparsity matters.
caption.3: Readout_k = max(0, ⟨a, d_k⟩ − t). Adjacent pentagon directions overlap by cos 72° ≈ 0.31, so a threshold above that silences a lone feature's interference, at the price of shrinking every true reading by t.

where_else: Linear probes: a learned direction that reads one feature out of the residual stream
Steering vectors: add a feature direction to push the model's behaviour
Sparse autoencoders: learn an overcomplete dictionary of feature directions

hamming.what: A direction in a model's activation space that corresponds to something a human can name.
hamming.when: Whenever you try to read, find or change what a model represents, from probes to sparse autoencoders to steering.
hamming.why: Neurons are often polysemantic and there can be more features than dimensions, so directions, not neurons, are the unit that carries meaning.

object.title: The bearing cloud
object.subtitle: Dots are activations; arrows are feature bearings that ignore the neuron axes.

cap.1: Each dot is one activation: one token's spot on the map. Dots from French text gather in one place, dots from code in another.
cap.2: Each point is a residual-stream vector; contexts that share a property cluster along a common direction.
cap.3: Activations for inputs sharing a feature have a shared component along that feature's direction.

cap.1: The arrows are feature bearings. They don't run along the axes, so no single neuron is 'the French neuron'.
cap.2: Feature directions are not basis vectors; each one mixes many neuron coordinates.
cap.3: In a non-privileged basis there is no reason for feature directions to be axis-aligned.

cap.1: The sheet holds every spot with zero French reading. How far a dot sits off the sheet, along the arrow, is how French it is.
cap.2: The plane is the set of activations whose projection onto the French direction is 0.
cap.3: The hyperplane ⟨a, d⟩ = 0; signed distance from it along d is the feature's activation.

cap.1: French plus code lands where the two arrows add up. Adding a bearing moves a spot: steering in miniature.
cap.2: If features are directions, co-occurring features add, and adding a direction to an activation writes that feature in.
cap.3: Linear representation implies additivity: a + α·d_French shifts the French reading by α, the premise of activation steering.

predict.q: A neuron fires on two unrelated things. What is the safest conclusion?

options.t: It's polysemantic: look for feature directions rather than trusting the neuron
It proves the model stores two features in superposition

predict.why: Polysemanticity is an observation. Superposition is one hypothesis about it, not a synonym.

predict.q: How do you read how much of a feature an activation holds?

options.t: Project it onto the feature's direction

predict.why: Features are directions, and they need not line up with any single neuron.

predict.q: Five features share a two-dimensional space. What is the price?

options.t: Interference: reading one picks up a little of the others
Nothing, as long as training runs long enough

predict.why: Five directions in two dimensions can't all be perpendicular; sparse data keeps the cost rarely paid.

object.where: Anywhere meaning lives in directions: probe weights, steering vectors, SAE latents.
